planting.note: Take tip cuttings that include some green leaf tissue rather than an all-white section, since the cream-colored portions of the leaf lack chlorophyll and cannot sustain rooting on their own.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10-12, in a well-drained potting mix that is allowed to dry slightly between waterings. This sport of the species baby rubber plant carries broad, irregular cream-to-yellow margins around a gray-green leaf center, giving it a brighter, more decorative look than the solid dark-green species. Because reduced chlorophyll slows growth, it stays slightly more compact than the straight species and needs more light than an all-green plant to keep its variegation from fading. Propagate from stem or leaf-petiole cuttings, choosing sections that retain some green tissue for reliable rooting.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist mix or water; keep in bright indirect light immediately after rooting, since low light causes the gold marbling to fade back toward plain green.

directions: Site in bright, curtain-filtered light indoors, or in dappled shade outdoors in zones 10-12, using a fast-draining potting mix and allowing the surface to dry between waterings. Golden Gate is grown for its irregular, marbled splashes of gold and green across each thick, glossy leaf, a bolder and more random pattern than the clean cream-edged look of 'Variegata'. Like other obtusifolia forms it stores water in its fleshy leaves and tolerates missed waterings far better than overwatering. Increase light levels if new growth starts emerging solid green, which signals the plant is reverting toward the species type.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Purpusii Wandering Jew (Solid Purple Inch Plant)

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem tip cuttings in water or moist mix; once rooted, pinch growing tips periodically to keep the trailing stems dense rather than long and sparse.

directions: Grow in partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained soil; unlike the common zebrina, this selection (originally described as Zebrina purpusii) lacks the paired silvery bands and instead shows larger, uniformly bronze-purple leaves with plum undersides. Its bigger leaves and more robust stems give it a coarser, denser look in hanging baskets or as a groundcover than the classic striped form. It roots readily wherever a stem node touches soil, so contain it in beds where spreading is undesirable. Provide bright but indirect light to keep the purple pigment intense, since deep shade dulls the coloring toward green.

common_name: Tricolor Wandering Jew (Pink-and-White Striped Small-Leaf Spiderwort)

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings in water or moist mix; discard any stems that revert to solid green, since removing them keeps the clump's variegated color from being crowded out.

directions: Plant in partial shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil or a hanging container; this small-leaf spiderwort selection layers pink and cream striping over green, giving it a softer, more pastel look than the plain white-striped 'Variegata'. It is somewhat less vigorous and more prone to reverting to plain green in low light than either the species or 'Variegata', so bright indirect light helps hold the pink tones. Trailing stems root at the nodes wherever they touch soil, making it easy to propagate or to fill in a groundcover patch. Pinch stems regularly to keep growth compact and encourage fuller, more colorful new foliage.

planting.note: Plant small scaly rhizomes 1 inch deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this subspecies can be left in the ground year-round in zones 7-10 and goes summer-dormant like the typical purple shamrock.

directions: Plant rhizomes in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this named subspecies of purple shamrock is separated from the typical form by its leaflet tips, which are more deeply notched into a distinct two-lobed, butterfly-wing shape rather than a simple triangular point. Its flowers also differ, opening pale lilac-white with a darker purple throat instead of the uniform pink of the common purple shamrock. Like the species, the folded burgundy leaflets close at night and in bright sun, reopening each morning. It suits the same containers, window boxes, and shaded border edgings as the common purple shamrock, and the foliage is likewise edible in small amounts due to its oxalic acid content.

common_name: Hawaiian Spider Plant (Solid Chartreuse Curly Spider Plant)

planting.note: Pot up rooted plantlets or divisions any time indoors, or move containers to a shaded porch after last frost; give brighter light than the variegated forms need, since without white striping this cultivar relies on more light to keep its chartreuse color vivid rather than fading toward dull green.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile potting mix, letting the top inch of soil dry between waterings. Unlike the white-striped 'Vittatum' and 'Variegatum' or the curly-variegated 'Bonnie', 'Hawaiian' carries solid, bright chartreuse-green leaves with a gently wavy margin and no white striping at all, giving it a warmer, more uniform glow than the other spider plant selections. It sends out the same long, arching stolons bearing plantlets that can be potted up or left trailing for a cascading display. Flush the pot occasionally with distilled or rain water to prevent the tan leaf-tip burn that fluoride and salts in tap water can cause on this and other spider plant forms.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Chlorophytum comosum
